talk: A multiple is a shortcut for valuing a business: take a profit number and multiply it by what similar businesses sell for. If similar clubs sell for 8 times their EBITDA, yours is probably worth around 8 times too. The hard parts are picking the right multiple and remembering that debt comes off before the owners get paid.

terms.meaning: What buyers pay for each dollar of profit, like 8 times EBITDA.
What the whole business is worth, before paying off debt.
What's left for the owners after the debt is paid off.

questions.prompt: Similar clubs sell for 8 times EBITDA. Your EBITDA is $3.5M. What's the whole club worth (its enterprise value)?
whyNot: $3.5M is one year of EBITDA. Buyers pay a multiple of it.
That adds the multiple instead of multiplying by it. $3.5M x 8 = $28M.
$3.5M x 10 = $35M uses a multiple of 10. Similar clubs sell for 8.

questions.prompt: The club has $10M of loans. If a buyer pays $28M for the whole club, how much do the owners get?
working: The loans are paid off first.
whyNot: $10M is the loans. That goes to the lenders, not the owners.
$28M is the whole club. The lenders get their $10M first.
$28M + $10M = $38M adds the debt. Debt is money the club owes, so it comes off.

questions.prompt: Two clubs both make $3.5M of EBITDA. One is growing fast with loyal fans. The other is shrinking. A seller asks 8 times EBITDA for each. Which is the better buy?
questions.hint: What happens to each club's profit next year?
working: Same EBITDA today, so both cost $3.5M x 8 = $28M.
The growing club's EBITDA should rise, so you pay less for each dollar of future profit.
Multiples price the future, not just this year. Growth and loyal customers earn a higher multiple.
whyNot: The shrinking club's profit is heading down. At the same price you get less profit each year.
Same price today, but not the same future. The growing club should earn more in the years ahead.
Multiples work fine as a shortcut. The skill is adjusting them for growth and risk.

penalty.prompt: Similar clubs sell for {mult} times EBITDA. Your EBITDA is {ebitda} and you owe {debt}. How much would the owners get if the club sold?
penalty.hint: EBITDA times the multiple, then pay off the loans.
working: {ebitda} x {mult} = {ebitda * mult|usd} for the whole club.
{ebitda * mult|usd} - {debt} = {ebitda * mult - debt|usd} for the owners.

traps.why: That's the whole club. The lenders get their {debt} first.
Debt is money the club owes, so it comes off.

call.title: The end-of-season pot
call.prompt: There's $300,000 to spend before the summer. A squad bonus should keep morale up and bring 200 more fans. The academy and a youth stand should bring 1,000 more fans.

options.label: Pay a squad bonus
options.result: 200 x $18 = $3,600 a matchday back on $300,000. Nice for morale, poor for value.

options.label: Invest in the academy
options.result: Good call. 1,000 x $18 = $18,000 a matchday, so $300,000 / $18,000 = about 17 matchdays to pay back. Growing profit also earns a bigger multiple when the club is valued.

options.label: Keep it in the bank
options.result: Cash sitting still doesn't grow the club, and buyers pay for growth.

takeaway: A business is worth a multiple of its profit, minus its debt. Growth earns a bigger multiple.
